summary:
We focused on six lunar locations, gathering official NASA data from QuickMap, Moon Trek, and JPL Horizons (for azimuth and elevation), backed by research papers to master the project's physical and astronomical aspects. We integrated our physical calculations into an intuitive, interactive tool designed for space missions, accessible to users of all ages and expertise levels, including astronauts. Currently, we are working to expand coverage to the entire lunar surface using the LRO/LOLA dataset, which time constraints prevented in this phase.
The tool enables interactive site comparisons across customizable mission dates and durations, providing vital metrics:
• Illumination ratios and sunlight duration.
• Earth communication windows and maximum signal-loss periods.
• Return-trip scheduling.
• A 2D simulation allowing users to adjust parameters like azimuth and time.
Future plans include an interactive educational program for students that simulates space missions, challenging them to rapidly adjust landing sites under time pressure to spark their passion for astronomy and exploration.
details:
We focused on six specific locations, gathering data from "QuickMap" and incorporating the necessary layers via "Moon Trek." We also retrieved temporal and angular data—such as azimuth and elevation—from "JPL Horizons." All of this information is derived from official NASA data. Furthermore, we consulted various research papers and sources to better understand the physical and astronomical aspects of the project. We performed the required physical calculations and integrated them into a functional, interactive tool accessible to anyone, regardless of age or level of astronomical expertise; it is also fully suitable for use by astronauts. We are currently working on future enhancements to cover the entire lunar surface by incorporating comprehensive surface data (from the LRO/LOLA dataset)—a task for which we lacked sufficient time during this phase. The tool is designed to be fully operational for future space missions. It offers several features, including interactive site comparisons and the ability to freely select mission dates and durations. These comparisons provide essential details, such as illumination ratios, duration of sunlight, communication windows with Earth (including the longest periods of signal loss), and return-trip scheduling. Additionally, the tool includes a 2D simulation that models these dynamics, allowing users to adjust parameters like azimuth and time. We have ensured that the interface design is intuitive and well-suited for space mission environments. Looking ahead, we plan to develop an interactive educational program that illustrates these phenomena for students, simulating space missions by challenging them to rapidly adjust landing sites under time pressure—an approach designed to ignite their passion for exploration and astronomy.

We made optimal use of AI to identify new phenomena in space science; we also utilized it to clarify certain complex aspects within our data sources. Our coding members used AI to Debug our frontend and backend codes against the errors that appeared.

The Lunar site navigator browser is a project that gives the user a simple version of the more complicated datasets and websites, making it easier for professionals to make last minute changes in the landing areas based on the sunlight and Earth connectivity durations, and easier for non-professionals to navigate and understand the landing sites without further explanation.

Users interact with a labeled NASA Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO) South Pole terrain map featuring official candidate regions (such as Malapert Massif, Mons Mouton, Nobile Rim, and Haworth) or input custom lunar coordinates by putting in the Latitude and Longitude and ln of them. Selecting a site triggers our comparison side, which computes T+0 solar elevation angles, total sunlight percentages, Earth-link communication ratios, maximum eclipse durations, and forward prospective countdowns across customizable mission windows (14 to 30 days). Below the telemetry cards, a dynamic 2D SVG horizon visualizer plots 360-degree terrain ridge silhouettes against real-time Sun and Earth azimuths, complete with interactive time sliders, zoom controls. So the user can have easy eye comparison free from typical spreadsheets and boring stream of info.

Frontend & Rendering: HTML5, CSS3, Vanilla JavaScript (ES6+), and custom dynamic Scalable Vector Graphics (SVG) for real-time horizon geometry.

Data & Prototyping: Python (used during development for coordinate validation and prototyping orbital equations) alongside official NASA LRO / Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter (LOLA) South Pole topographical reference datasets.
